## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why must the highest-capacity deliberative models on an embodied robot operate at the slowest frequencies, and how can a machine survive the cognitive latency of thought?_

An embodied robot operating in unstructured human environments requires deep semantic scene decomposition, multimodal spatial grounding, and long-horizon causal reasoning—capabilities delivered by modern vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models containing billions of parameters. In data center machine learning systems, throughput is maximized by aggregating user requests into massive batches ($B = 64\text{--}256$), driving matrix-matrix multiplications deep into the compute-bound regime of the Roofline model. In physical AI, however, the system commands exactly one physical plant in real time: the architecture is locked into the **embodied batch size 1 constraint** ($B = 1$). At batch size 1, transformer matrix multiplications collapse into memory-bandwidth-bound matrix-vector operations ($\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$), where each weight parameter must be fetched from off-chip memory for every forward step.

Even on flagship edge System-on-Chips (SoCs) equipped with wide LPDDR5 memory interfaces, streaming a 7-billion-parameter model footprint ($14\,\text{GB}$ in FP16) across the bus bounds fresh inference cadence by the memory wall ($f \le B_{\text{mem}} / M_{\text{weights}} \approx 10\text{--}44\,\text{Hz}$). Meanwhile, the physical machine continues moving through continuous space, where rejecting unexpected contact disturbances, preventing joint torque windup, and stabilizing moving mass require deterministic feedback loops operating at $1000\,\text{Hz}$ ($1\,\text{ms}$). A physical AI architecture cannot afford to let high-level neural deliberation directly close the low-level motor loop. Granting a 7B+ model direct executive authority over motor inverters would leave the physical plant unguided for tens to hundreds of milliseconds between inference passes, courting catastrophic collisions.

Instead, the embodied Brain must act as an asynchronous, unprivileged proposer. Deliberation is decoupled from physical execution: the foundation model evaluates periodically to predict prospective trajectory segments across a receding horizon, using **action chunking** ($H = 16\text{--}64$) to amortize off-chip DRAM weight transfers across physical wall-clock time. Iterative generative refinement (such as $K = 10\text{--}16$ diffusion denoising steps) executes strictly on a compact action head ($\sim 50\,\text{M}$ parameters) whose entire footprint fits within on-chip SRAM cache, bypassing the off-chip memory wall during iterative sampling. Downstream, deterministic safety runtimes running at $1000\,\text{Hz}$ on isolated safety silicon enforce physical invariants, arbitrating execution permission or executing graceful fallbacks. This chapter examines the hardware constraints, memory hierarchies, tokenization costs, and action-chunking mechanisms of the embodied Brain, revealing how high-capacity foundation models can safely direct physical work without stalling the real-time reflexes necessary for survival.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare classical analytical pipelines and learned representations on coverage, sensory robustness, and formal verifiability
- Calculate the memory wall bound on a model's fresh-evaluation rate ($f \le B_{\text{mem}} / M_{\text{weights}}$) under the embodied batch size 1 constraint
- Estimate key-value cache expansion from multi-camera tokenization, hidden dimensions, and retained history windows
- Explain how action chunking ($H$) amortizes off-chip weight transfers over physical wall-clock time without improving closed-loop reaction latency
- Contrast SRAM-resident diffusion action head decoding with off-chip foundation model backbone weight sweeps
- Apply replanning period, inference latency, and target drift to size an action chunk for a dynamic target
- Diagnose cognitive failure modes: semantic hallucinations, uncalibrated softmax overconfidence, perceptual chattering, and expired intent leases
- Formulate the formal Proposal Record schema ($\mathcal{P}$) and evaluate why unprivileged deliberative proposals require independent real-time verification

:::

## The Embodied Brain {#sec-brain-embodied}

In @sec-body, the Physical Body established the physical envelope of moving mass, codifying its continuous torque ceilings ($\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{cont}}$), thermal dissipation limits ($I_{\text{rms}} \le I_{\text{cont}}$), bus voltage sag thresholds, and stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}}$) into the **Limit Record** ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{body}}$, @sec-body-measuring-limits). A warehouse mobile manipulator can operate strictly within every boundary documented in that Limit Record—motor drives well within continuous torque ratings, the power distribution network holding nominal voltage, and joint velocities below physical ceilings—yet still fail at a task as ordinary as grasping an unfamiliar ceramic mug from a moving conveyor and handing it to a human coworker. The machine drops the object or crushes the ceramic rim because low-level motor physics cannot determine what the object is, where its structural affordances lie, or how to navigate around dynamic obstacles. In disembodied machine learning, an erroneous token or latency hiccup simply stalls a text generation stream. In physical AI, a cognitive proposal commands physical actuators that directly accelerate moving mass possessing kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q}) \mathbf{v}$). An invalid or delayed proposal can breach physical limits, and collisions cannot be rolled back (the first bedrock law, @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws).

Because an embodied agent commands exactly one physical plant in real time, the architecture is constrained to the **embodied batch size 1 constraint** ($B=1$). In data center ML systems, batching amortizes weight fetching across dozens or hundreds of concurrent sequences, elevating arithmetic intensity ($I = \text{FLOPs/byte}$) into the compute-bound regime. At $B=1$, however, neural network execution collapses into memory-bandwidth-bound matrix-vector operations ($\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$), requiring every single weight parameter to be transferred from off-chip DRAM across the memory bus for each forward step.

For a modern 7-billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation model stored in 16-bit floating point precision (FP16, $M_{\text{weights}} = 14\,\text{GB}$), sustained memory bandwidth on mobile edge SoCs ($B_{\text{mem}} \approx 140\text{--}204\,\text{GB/s}$) limits fresh inference cadence to:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}} \approx 10\text{--}44\,\text{Hz}$$
even before accounting for vision tokenization, multi-head attention over historical context, or kernel dispatch overheads. This physical ceiling stands orders of magnitude below the deterministic millisecond servo cadences ($1000\,\text{Hz}$) required to close field-oriented current loops, stabilize mechanical linkages against contact shocks, and prevent destructive torque windup. If a multi-billion-parameter model were granted direct executive authority over motor inverters, the physical plant would drift unguided for tens to hundreds of milliseconds between inference passes, courting catastrophic kinetic failure.

The Brain is therefore mathematically and physically forced to operate as an unprivileged deliberation engine that may only propose (\ref{dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary}). This architectural separation organizes the machine into a **two-speed brain architecture**\index{Two-speed brain architecture!hybrid control} (@fig-two-speed-brain). At the deliberative tier, high-capacity foundation models perform slow cognition at $1\text{--}50\,\text{Hz}$ on the application processor (GPU/NPU), ingesting multimodal camera streams and natural language instructions to emit structured trajectory proposals. At the real-time tier, deterministic safety monitors execute at $1000\,\text{Hz}$ on isolated safety silicon, evaluating candidate proposals against physical limits before granting execution permission ($u^*$), or asserting an asynchronous refusal that triggers deliberative state resynchronization. On the mobile manipulator, this deliberative tier hosts two complementary learned proposers: an intent model that revises coarse goals at $1\text{--}5\,\text{Hz}$, and a compact action chunk policy that emits dense sequences of future setpoints at $10\text{--}50\,\text{Hz}$. The permission path arbitrates every candidate waypoint, ensuring that safety-critical invariants hold regardless of neural inference jitter, latency spikes, or perceptual failures.

A learned proposer earns its place by doing what hand-authored geometry cannot. It parses open-vocabulary natural language directives, extracts spatial affordances from high-entropy unstructured scenes, tolerates specular glare and occlusions that break analytical filters, and anchors visual detections to metric $SE(3)$ coordinates the manipulator can physically reach. Yet every parameter added to achieve open-world generalization exacts a direct toll in memory bus traffic and inference latency.

@Fig-cadence-gap formalizes this hardware tension across embodied workload classes: as parameter capacity scales from compact micro-controllers to multi-billion-parameter foundation models, achievable evaluation cadence drops precipitously along a memory-bandwidth-governed Pareto frontier. Workloads that carry the largest parameter footprints update least frequently, operating multiple orders of magnitude below the physical control rates required to maintain continuous dynamic balance and joint compliance. The systems engineering question is therefore what a learned proposer can deliver on time, how the memory hierarchy (SRAM vs. DRAM) dictates achievable proposal cadence, and how action chunking bridges this cognitive latency gap without sacrificing physical stability.

::: {#fig-cadence-gap fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Cadence regimes**: Parameter counts and example update rates for different control, vision, and embodied workloads. The points are illustrative workload regimes rather than runs on a common device, and parameter count alone does not determine update rate." fig-alt="Log-log scatter of parameter counts and example update rates for different workload classes, with shaded control and deliberation rate bands."}

@Sec-brain-classical-wall shows why pipelines built on hand-authored geometry and state machines lose coverage outside the factory cell, and @sec-brain-learned-representations shows what learned representations recover and what they cost in tokens and memory traffic. @Sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline turns that cost into the machine's numbers: the memory wall that bounds how often its intent model can run, the action chunking that keeps the arm supplied between evaluations, and the drift that bounds how long each chunk stays true. @Sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities then takes up the ways a proposal can arrive on time and still be wrong, each of which leaves the permission path with a proposal it must be able to refuse.

## The Classical Wall {#sec-brain-classical-wall}

For nearly a century, automated control and robotics approached cognition as an explicit geometric and analytical physics problem [@wiener1948cybernetics; @kalman1960new; @craig2005introduction]. Under this classical paradigm, engineers constructed mathematical representations from first principles.

Engineers used analytical kinematics and differential dynamics to map desired end-effector[^fn-hw-end-effector] motions into actuator torques using closed-form equations.[^fn-math-classical-dynamics] On standard microprocessors, evaluating these analytical equations requires negligible compute: recursive Newton-Euler dynamics and convex quadratic programs (QPs) for operational space control execute with deterministic sub-millisecond latency ($< 100\,\mu\text{s}$ on a single CPU core for $D \le 7$ degrees of freedom). Perception relied on matching hand-crafted 3D Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models against sensor point clouds using geometric alignment algorithms, such as iterative closest point (ICP) or random sample consensus (RANSAC). High-level task logic was authored as explicit Boolean state machines that dictated deterministic transitions between operational phases, such as approaching, aligning, grasping, and retracting.

[^fn-hw-end-effector]: **End-Effector**\index{End-effector!definition}: The active tool, gripper, or hand at the distal tip of a robotic manipulator that interacts directly with physical workpieces and the environment.

[^fn-math-classical-dynamics]: **Rigid-Body Dynamics Formulation**\index{Rigid-body dynamics!Euler-Lagrange formulation}\index{Equations of motion!manipulator dynamics}: Classical control computes generalized torques via the standard manipulator equation $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$, where $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ represents the configuration-dependent inertia matrix, $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})$ captures Coriolis and centripetal terms, and $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$ accounts for gravitational loading. Specifically, $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ captures configuration-dependent mass moments: extending an articulated linkage shifts mass outward from the rotational axes, increasing reflected rotational inertia ($I \propto m r^2$) and demanding quadratically higher joint torque for equivalent angular acceleration. This analytical formulation becomes computationally intractable and physically inaccurate when machines interact with unmodeled frictional contacts, fluid drag, or deformable objects. Derivations are provided in @sec-appendix-control.

::: {#fig-industrial-welding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Industrial spot-welding workcell**: Multiple six-degree-of-freedom articulated robots execute preprogrammed spot welding paths on stamped automotive chassis at the BMW Leipzig plant. Operating in a calibrated factory environment with submillimeter repeatable fixtures and safety interlock cages, classical controllers provide deterministic cycle timing and formal stability proofs. (Credit: BMW Group / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0 de)." fig-alt="Articulated industrial robots executing automated spot welding on an automotive chassis within a safety-caged factory cell."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_industrial_welding.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Where the operational environment is strictly structured and bounded (@fig-industrial-welding), classical methods provide dependable behavior within their modeled conditions. On an automated automotive assembly line, an industrial robot welds stamped steel panels where every workpiece arrives at an exact coordinate within sub-millimeter tolerances. Ambient lighting is tightly regulated by industrial fixtures, and human workers are excluded by physical interlock safety fences. Within the causal boundary defined in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, this controlled regime permits explicit models, bounded servo timing, and formal Lyapunov stability analysis under stated assumptions. Engineers can verify trajectory tracking error bounds ($\lVert \mathbf{e}(t) \rVert \le \epsilon$) and certify controller software coverage against safety standards without collecting empirical demonstrations.

Yet when an embodied machine leaves the structured factory cage to operate in unstructured open-world environments (@fig-unstructured-rescue), this analytical paradigm hits the **classical wall** [@brooks1991intelligence; @levine2018learning]. The physical world is not a sterile CAD drawing; it is continuous, deformable, and endlessly variable.

::: {#fig-unstructured-rescue fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Unstructured search-and-rescue robot**: A tracked mobile robot navigates an obstacle course with irregular inclines, loose debris, and visual occlusions. In such unmapped environments, preauthored geometric models and rigid state machines can lose coverage; learned policies may help infer spatial affordances and traversability from sensory streams. (Credit: TU Darmstadt Rescue Robotics / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0)." fig-alt="Tracked mobile robot traversing irregular rubble and wooden obstacles in an unstructured search-and-rescue test arena."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_unstructured_rescue.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

The classical paradigm suffers from three fundamental architectural breakdowns when confronting real-world entropy:

1. **Combinatorial explosion of explicit geometry:** In a commercial logistics warehouse handling millions of retail stock keeping units (SKUs), authoring CAD models, surface meshes, and grasp wrench spaces for every deformable garment, wrapped bottle, and cardboard box is intractable. Classical pose estimation matches dense point clouds ($N \sim 10^5$ points) against pre-indexed CAD templates using nearest-neighbor searches ($O(M \cdot N \log N)$ across $M$ candidate templates). This search space explodes under object variation, and algorithms fail entirely when encountering non-rigid bodies whose continuous deformation states possess infinite degrees of freedom.
2. **Sensory brittleness of hand-crafted feature filters:** Classical vision pipelines rely on hand-tuned geometric filters (such as Sobel edge detectors, Harris corner response matrices, or surface-normal clustering thresholds). Under specular reflections, dynamic shadows, motion blur, or dust, optical gradients flip unpredictably. A single missing depth discontinuity can cause Euclidean planar segmentation to fuse two separate workpieces into an imaginary hybrid geometry, causing the motion planner to propose an end-effector grasp in empty air.
3. **State-space explosion of hand-authored Boolean logic:** Finite state machines require human engineers to anticipate and explicitly code every transition between discrete operational states. Across $K$ operational variables and environmental conditions, the required state-transition graph scales exponentially ($O(2^K)$ or $O(S^K)$). When an uncataloged physical edge case occurs—such as a slightly scuffed package barcode, a slipped conveyor belt, or an unexpected human hand reaching into the workspace—the state machine encounters an undefined transition, stalling execution or commanding an inappropriate motion.

Learned representations overcome these breakdowns by replacing brittle geometric discretizations and hand-authored state branches with continuous, high-dimensional neural function approximation ($\mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} \to \mathbb{R}^d$). By training on web-scale multimodal data and real-world teleoperated demonstrations, neural networks learn spatial affordances, semantic invariants, and compliance-aware manipulation directly from sensory distributions.

However, for an ML systems architect, this capability shift fundamentally transforms the compute and memory profile of the machine. The robot trades predictable, sub-millisecond, CPU-resident analytical loops ($< 1\,\text{MB}$ memory footprint, $O(1)$ determinism) for massive, memory-bandwidth-bound neural workloads that stream gigabytes of parameters across off-chip buses at batch size 1. Physical AI does not abandon classical control; rather, it encloses classical control inside learned semantic proposal loops, retaining analytical stability proofs and high-frequency disturbance rejection at the inner $1000\,\text{Hz}$ servo tier while delegating open-world geometric discovery to neural representations.

## Learned Representations {#sec-brain-learned-representations}

Asked to take the unfamiliar ceramic mug from the conveyor, a classical pipeline needs a CAD model, a feature threshold, and a state-machine branch that nobody wrote for this object. A learned model trained on many graspable objects can propose the handle as a grasp region from pixels and a sentence of instruction. Physical AI extends classical pipelines with such neural representations wherever hand-authored models lose coverage, and four pillars support the shift:

1. **Open-world semantic generalizability:** Classical controllers are geometrically precise but semantically blind: an inverse kinematics solver can expertly drive an end-effector to coordinate $(x, y, z)$, yet it possesses zero understanding of whether that location contains a sturdy mug or a fragile glass, or how surrounding objects relate to human tasks. Modern vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models project open-vocabulary natural language instructions and high-resolution camera streams into shared semantic embedding spaces ($d = 2048\text{--}4096$) [@driess2023palme; @brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. When commanded to "wipe the coffee spill from the counter and stow the mug in the drying rack," a trained model extracts affordance heatmaps and proposes task-relevant target poses without requiring an explicit CAD model or hand-coded primitive.
2. **Empirical sensory robustness:** Hand-authored visual thresholds can flip under changing illumination or texture. Learned representations extract distributed feature hierarchies that tolerate specular glare, ambient shadow transitions, and partial camera occlusions when training distributions cover them. However, because neural representations are continuous non-linear approximations, their outputs lack global Lipschitz bounds under severe out-of-distribution shift.
3. **Multi-contact and deformable dynamics:** Many physical manipulation tasks (folding textiles, routing flexible wire harnesses through automotive door assemblies, or scooping granular media) involve non-smooth contact mechanics, variable Coulomb friction, and infinite-dimensional deformations that cannot be modeled in closed-form differential equations. With suitable contact-rich teleoperated demonstrations and multi-modal sensory feedback (vision and proprioception), neural policies learn compliance-aware behavioral manifolds that reduce contact forces against unexpected mechanical resistance.
4. **Empirical scaling with data and compute:** In accordance with the bitter lesson highlighted in @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws, policy performance scales with training demonstration diversity and compute capacity (@fig-aloha-manipulator) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Yet on an embodied machine, this empirical scaling collides directly with the physical constraints of onboard electrical power, thermal dissipation envelopes ($30\text{--}60\,\text{W}$ for mobile edge compute), and memory streaming bandwidth.

Each of these gains holds only where training and test data cover the operating conditions, and none of them bounds what the model proposes outside those conditions. That limit is why a learned output reaches the actuators only as a candidate proposal that the permission path may independently verify and refuse.

Rather than an opaque monolith, an embodied foundation model is a four-stage neural and systems pipeline (@fig-vla-taxonomy, @fig-vla-architecture) that transforms raw sensor streams into candidate motion proposals across explicit memory boundaries:

1. **Sensory Ingestion and Spatial Tokenization (The Inputs):**
   A vision transformer (ViT) frontend slices each incoming camera frame into a grid of non-overlapping pixel patches of size $P \times P$ (typically $14 \times 14$ or $16 \times 16$ pixels). Each patch is linearly projected into a vector of width $d$, augmented with 2D spatial sinusoidal positional embeddings, and tagged with a learned camera identifier.

   On a mobile manipulator equipped with three synchronized cameras (e.g., left wrist, right wrist, and an overhead torso mount) capturing $224 \times 224$ images, each frame yields $(224 / 14)^2 = 256$ spatial patches. Across three cameras, ingestion injects $3 \times 256 = 768$ visual tokens into the model's sequence on every perceptual step. When concatenated with tokenized natural language commands ($\sim 32$ tokens) and proprioceptive joint state embeddings ($\sim 16$ tokens), the initial context sequence length exceeds $S \approx 800$ tokens. In FP16 precision ($2\,\text{bytes}$ per element) with hidden dimension $d = 4096$, the initial token embedding matrix alone occupies:
   $$M_{\text{embed}} = S \times d \times 2\,\text{bytes} = 800 \times 4096 \times 2 \approx 6.55\,\text{MB}$$
   Crucially, 2D image coordinates and attention patterns do not constitute metric depth: projecting an end-effector into physical 3D space requires calibrated extrinsic camera matrices and depth telemetry.

2. **Multimodal Alignment and Attention (The Backbone):**
   The token sequence passes through $L = 32$ transformer layers where multi-head self-attention computes pairwise token interactions. The computational cost of full self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length ($O(S^2 d)$ FLOPs), while the Key-Value (KV) cache that retains prior token states for autoregressive context expands linearly ($O(L \cdot S \cdot d)$):
   $$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times L \times d \times S \times \text{bytes}$$
   For a 32-layer model with $d = 4096$ using FP16 storage, each context token claims $2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2 = 524{,}288\,\text{bytes} \approx 0.524\,\text{MB}$ of KV cache. Reading this KV cache across off-chip DRAM on every token step creates massive memory bus traffic that directly competes with weight streaming. Furthermore, strong attention weights between language tokens (such as "mug handle") and visual patches do not prove geometric affordance or collision-free clearance; nor does the KV cache track object permanence during physical occlusions. The formal patch-embedding, position-encoding, and attention formulations appear in @sec-appendix-ml-patch-embedding.

3. **Specialized Action Decoders (The Outputs):**
   Instead of generating open-ended conversational text, the final hidden representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is routed to specialized action decoders. While vision-language navigation (VLN) models emit topological waypoints or heading rates $(v_t, \omega_t)$ (@fig-vln-navigation), manipulation (VLA) models diverge sharply in how they bridge semantic representations to physical motion:

   * *Discrete Categorical Tokenization (RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA):* Early VLAs cast continuous robot control as discrete language modeling by quantizing each action dimension into $B = 256$ uniform bins [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]:
     $$\text{bin}(a_k) = \left\lfloor \frac{a_k - a_{\min}}{a_{\max} - a_{\min}} \times 255 \right\rfloor \in [0, 255]$$
     Each bin maps to a discrete token in the vocabulary. While this directly reuses pretrained language transformer heads, it introduces severe systems bottlenecks. Generating a 7-DoF action vector requires seven sequential autoregressive forward steps. At batch size 1, sequential decoding exposes **GPU kernel launch latency**: each step dispatches hundreds of small layer operations (LayerNorm, Softmax, GEMV, GeLU). On edge SoCs, driver launch overhead ($\approx 5\text{--}15\,\mu\text{s}$ per kernel) dominates execution time when tensor sizes are small, stalling execution units on CPU-GPU dispatch queues and ballooning latency beyond $150\text{--}300\,\text{ms}$. Furthermore, 256-bin discretization imposes a coarse spatial resolution: across a $2\pi\,\text{rad}$ joint range, each bin spans $\Delta a \approx 1.4^\circ$. At the tip of a 1-meter manipulator, a single bin increment causes an instantaneous spatial step of $\Delta x \approx 1.0\,\text{m} \times (1.4 \times \pi / 180) \approx 24.4\,\text{mm}$. When attempting precision assembly or grasping fragile glassware, this spatial quantization forces high-gain joint controllers to chatter violently against contact surfaces.

   * *Continuous Generative Action Chunking (Octo, $\pi_0$, ACT, Diffusion Policy):* To eliminate sequential tokenization bottlenecks, modern policies couple the transformer backbone with continuous generative decoders [@chi2024diffusionpolicy; @octo_2023; @black2024pi0]. Standard continuous regression trained with mean squared error (MSE) loss fails on multimodal human demonstrations: when demonstrators choose either a left or right detour around an obstacle with equal probability, an MSE objective forces the network to predict the conditional expectation—the arithmetic mean of the two trajectories—directing the robot straight into a collision. Generative heads resolve mode averaging by sampling continuous trajectory chunks:
     $$\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a} \quad (H = 16\text{--}64\text{ steps})$$
     Action chunking amortizes weight transfer by reusing a single perceptual backbone forward pass over an entire horizon of future waypoints. Crucially, in diffusion and flow-matching policies, the iterative refinement steps ($K = 10\text{--}16$ denoising passes) execute **strictly on the lightweight action head** (typically $\sim 50\text{M}$ parameters, which occupies $< 100\,\text{MB}$ and fits entirely within on-chip SRAM cache), **never** on the massive 7B-parameter VLA backbone. The multi-billion-parameter backbone is evaluated only once per replanning cycle, streaming its gigabytes of weights across DRAM just once every $T_{\text{replan}} = 50\text{--}200\text{ ms}$, while the on-chip head rapidly synthesizes the dense $H$-step trajectory chunk at high SRAM bandwidth ($> 1\text{--}2\,\text{TB/s}$) in $5\text{--}15\,\text{ms}$. That chunk is one candidate horizon, not a sequence of fresh observations. The next backbone evaluation must arrive before the accepted execution window expires; downstream interpolation and feedback run at their own rates.

4. **The Proposal Boundary (Isolation from Actuators):**
   Whether the model is a VLN mobility planner or a VLA manipulation policy, its output is a candidate proposal ($p_t$) on the unprivileged side of the proposal boundary (\ref{dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary}).\index{Unprivileged proposal!proposal boundary} Under the machine model of @sec-boundary-machine-model, the foundation model runs in user space on the application processor and has no path to the pulse-width modulation (PWM) registers or to the current in the motor coils.

   The design rule for this deliberative boundary is that learned models operating at the Brain's inference cadences ($1\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$) propose kinematic setpoints ($\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ or Cartesian poses), **never unbuffered, open-loop motor torques ($\boldsymbol{\tau}$)** directly to inverter switches. Motor torque is coupled to the plant through the manipulator equation of the classical-dynamics note in @sec-brain-classical-wall, plus a contact term $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{contact}}$. Because inertia $\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})$ and Coriolis forces $\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})$ vary non-linearly with instantaneous joint configuration and velocity, commanding open-loop torques, without high-frequency feedback, from a neural model that updates at tens of hertz at most can destabilize the limb when model error, friction, or payload variation is large enough.

   Kinematic setpoints, by contrast, specify an intended spatial path and leave high-gain closed-loop torque synthesis to the Body's drives, whose Field-Oriented Control (FOC) current loops run at $10\text{--}25\,\text{kHz}$ on dedicated motor inverter DSPs. Motor electromagnetic back-EMF, rotor inertia, and inverter dead times require feedback loops running at tens of kilohertz to close current and torque commands deterministically without thermal runaways or torque ripple. The electrical time constant of the motor windings ($\tau_e = L / R \approx 0.1\text{--}1.0\,\text{ms}$) demands sub-millisecond current regulation. Attempting to command raw motor torques from an asynchronous $20\,\text{Hz}$ neural policy across a $50\,\text{ms}$ open-loop horizon leads to catastrophic current spikes and motor thermal overloads whenever dynamic contact occurs. (Where specialized high-rate reinforcement learning policies operating at $100\text{--}500\text{ Hz}$ output torques directly, they still require an independently validated high-rate permission path, as @sec-nervous-invariant-checking argues; passivity checks for such torque streams are derived in @sec-appendix-control-passivity.)

::: {#dfn-brain-proposal-contract .callout-definition title="The proposal record"}

***The Proposal Record***\index{Proposal Record!definition}\index{Proposal contract!definition}\index{Proposal boundary!contract schema} ($\mathcal{P}$) is the typed data contract emitted across the proposal boundary from the unprivileged Brain to the real-time Nervous System. As the second formal record in the machine stack's 14-record contract lineage (following the Body's Limit Record and preceding the Nervous System's Transport Budget), it packages candidate trajectory setpoints, capture timestamps, evidence validity horizons, and provenance metadata for independent verification before execution permission is granted:
$$\mathcal{P} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, t_{\text{valid}}, H, \Delta t, \mathbf{Q}_{1:H}, \dot{\mathbf{Q}}_{1:H}, \mathbf{X}_{1:H}, \mathbf{g}_{1:H}, \text{model\_id}, \text{lease\_id}, \hat{p}, \text{crc} \rangle$$

1. **Significance**: By formalizing candidate motion into an explicit contract with capture timestamps and validity bounds, the Nervous System can reject stale or uncalibrated proposals before any setpoint reaches an actuator.
2. **Distinction**: Unlike an internal neural tensor, the Proposal Record is an immutable, verifiable boundary payload checked against physical invariant envelopes.
3. **Common pitfall**: Omitting observation timestamps or validity horizons, causing downstream controllers to execute delayed proposals computed from obsolete scene states.

:::

The data structure and verification rules defined in @tbl-03-proposal-record-schema govern every Proposal Record transmitted across the proposal boundary:

| Field         | Type            | Unit                    | Systems Semantics and Verification Rule                                                                    |
|:--------------|:----------------|:------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `t_capture`   | `uint64_t`      | $\text{ns}$             | Hardware timestamp of oldest sensory observation conditioning the proposal.                                |
| `t_valid`     | `uint64_t`      | $\text{ns}$             | Monotonic time after which proposal expires ($\le t_{\text{capture}} + \tau_{\text{ev}}$).                 |
| `horizon_H`   | `uint16_t`      | count                   | Number of prospective trajectory setpoints ($H = 16\text{--}64$).                                          |
| `delta_t`     | `uint32_t`      | $\mu\text{s}$           | Temporal interval between consecutive waypoints ($\Delta t = 20\,000\,\mu\text{s} \implies 50\text{ Hz}$). |
| `q_traj`      | `float32[H][D]` | $\text{rad}$            | Candidate joint trajectory array across $D$ degrees of freedom.                                            |
| `q_dot_traj`  | `float32[H][D]` | $\text{rad/s}$          | First derivative setpoints; verified for $C^1$ velocity continuity at chunk seam.                          |
| `x_cartesian` | `PoseSE3[H]`    | $\text{m}, \text{quat}$ | End-effector target poses; verified against workspace keep-out boundaries.                                 |
| `gripper_cmd` | `float32[H]`    | $[0, 1]$                | Gripper closure target; evaluated against grasp force and slip limits.                                     |
| `model_id`    | `uint32_t`      | hash                    | Cryptographic hash of model architecture, weights checkpoint, and calibration profile.                     |
| `confidence`  | `float32`       | $[0, 1]$                | Model reported confidence $\hat{p}$; compared against empirical ECE threshold.                             |
| `lease_id`    | `uint64_t`      | UUID                    | Identifier of active intent lease authorizing this operational phase.                                      |
| `crc32`       | `uint32_t`      | checksum                | Integrity checksum protecting shared-memory ring buffer payload.                                           |

: **The formal Proposal Record schema**: Data contract emitted across the proposal boundary from the unprivileged Brain to the real-time Nervous System. {#tbl-03-proposal-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[18,14,14,54]"}

:::

   Proposals reach the permission path through the handoff of @sec-nervous, and the permission path can refuse a hallucinated proposal when independent measurements, modeled limits, and a feasible fallback support that decision.[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]

[^fn-math-unprivileged-control]: **Proposal Boundary**\index{Proposal boundary!unprivileged proposals}: Treating the neural policy as an unprivileged proposal generator isolates stochastic inference from actuator registers. Candidate trajectory setpoints $\mathbf{q}_{\text{ref}}(t)$ are checked on dedicated safety silicon, so proposals that violate modeled actuator limits or keep-out regions can be rejected before any reaches a drive (@sec-nervous-actuation-authority).

Each neural stage of this pipeline is paid for in memory traffic. Every patch token must be attended over and held in the KV cache, and every evaluation of the backbone streams its weights from DRAM, so the capabilities this section described arrive at a rate the application processor sets rather than one the task chooses. On the mobile manipulator, that rate for its largest model falls well below the rate at which its arm consumes setpoints.

## Supply, Freshness, and the Memory Wall {#sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline}

At the pick station the mobile manipulator's arm consumes a new setpoint every few tens of milliseconds, while the mug it is reaching for keeps moving along the conveyor. Whatever model proposes those setpoints must settle two questions. The first is how often it can produce a proposal on the application processor the machine actually has; the second is how long each proposal stays true once the mug has moved. The answers explain why the machine carries two learned proposers rather than one.

After ingestion (the tokenization of @sec-brain-learned-representations), four stages turn those tokens into proposals (@fig-cognitive-pipeline), and Part III develops each one. Here they matter only for what each hands downstream and how quickly that goes stale.

On an edge robotics SoC operating with a **Unified Memory Architecture (UMA)**, physical memory bandwidth is a shared zero-sum resource. The CPU host cores, GPU/NPU matrix execution units, Image Signal Processors (ISPs), and Direct Memory Access (DMA) controllers all share a single physical LPDDR5 bus. Saturating this bus with gigabytes of neural weight streaming creates direct real-time safety hazards: when a multi-billion-parameter foundation model consumes $90\%$ of memory bus cycles, incoming high-bandwidth sensor streams (such as raw MIPI-CSI camera video and Ethernet LiDAR packets) suffer memory controller arbitration stalls. Internal hardware FIFO buffers overflow, dropping frames and blinding perception precisely while the machine is in motion.

Perception grounds what it recognizes in metric coordinates relative to the base, so that the mug becomes an $SE(3)$ pose and a graspable handle rather than an abstract semantic label;[^fn-brain-metric-grounding] its output ages from the moment of capture, and @sec-perception turns that age into a contract. Memory carries those estimates through occlusion and must let each one expire when the evidence behind it does (@sec-memory). Intent decomposes a task such as "take the ceramic mug off the conveyor and hand it to the coworker at the packing station" into subgoals, and because the mug moves while the intent model deliberates, it hands the planner a target that expires, an intent lease\index{Intent lease!temporal contract} (@sec-intent-lease). Planning converts that target into candidate setpoints for the base and the arm, the proposals the permission path will judge (@sec-planning). These stages, and the ingestion before them, all run on the application processor and draw on the same memory bus, which is where the machine's cadence is decided.

[^fn-brain-metric-grounding]: **Metric Spatial Grounding**\index{Metric spatial grounding}\index{Special Euclidean group!SE(3) grounding}: While disembodied AI operates over discrete semantic tokens, physical AI must ground those semantics in the Special Euclidean group $SE(3)$, mapping entities to metric distances (meters) and spatial orientations (quaternions) relative to the robot's base coordinate frame. Failing to maintain this metric grounding causes neural policies to emit kinematically impossible Cartesian paths that breach actuator workspace boundaries.

The flow ends at the proposal boundary, where the permission path evaluates each proposed action against real-time constraints and resources." fig-alt="Horizontal flowchart of the five-stage cognitive pipeline: Ingestion, Perception, Memory, Intent, and Planning, culminating at the proposal boundary."}
![](images/svg/fig03_cognitive_pipeline_horizontal.svg){width="95%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ High-throughput neural inference accelerators are isolated from deterministic cores in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

### The memory wall {#sec-brain-memory-wall}

The update cadence of an embodied neural policy is fundamentally governed by memory bandwidth rather than peak arithmetic capability. In high-performance computing, the **memory wall** defines the operational regime where computational execution units spend the vast majority of clock cycles stalled, waiting for operands to arrive from external memory. In physical AI, this architectural bottleneck is exacerbated by the strict real-time requirement to interact continuously with physical mass: while modern edge accelerator silicon delivers hundreds of teraflops of matrix multiplication performance, the physical interconnect pins and memory interfaces between the processor die and off-chip memory packages provide comparatively modest data transfer rates.

To understand the physical consequence of this bandwidth ceiling, consider what happens if a robot attempts to generate continuous motor actions one discrete step at a time through an autoregressive foundation model (such as a multi-billion-parameter VLA model). A model whose weights cannot remain on chip must stream them across the external DRAM bus once per evaluation. Operating under the **embodied batch size 1 constraint** ($B = 1$), the sustained memory bandwidth $B_{\text{mem}}$ and model weight footprint $M_{\text{weights}}$ strictly bound the maximum fresh-evaluation frequency:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}}$$
Even on flagship edge accelerators equipped with wide LPDDR5 or high-bandwidth memory (HBM) interfaces ($B_{\text{mem}} \approx 140\text{--}204\,\text{GB/s}$ sustained) executing quantized or compact 3B–7B policies ($M_{\text{weights}} \approx 4.6\text{--}14\,\text{GB}$), this bandwidth ceiling caps inference cadence at:
$$f \le \frac{B_{\text{mem}}}{M_{\text{weights}}} \approx 10\text{--}44\,\text{Hz}$$
before tokenization, multimodal attention, or decoding adds any latency. In single-step autoregressive generation, each action dimension requires predicting additional tokens; if each token revisits off-chip parameters, latency scales linearly with degrees of freedom. Because physical stabilization, joint impedance control, and reflex-level collision avoidance require deterministic update rates of $100\text{--}1000\,\text{Hz}$, **foundation models cannot serve as executive controllers in real-time physical loops**. They are physically trapped behind the memory wall, mathematically forcing an architecture where foundation models operate solely as unprivileged proposal engines. For detailed memory wall derivations and roofline hardware models, see @sec-appendix-systems.

This memory wall[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth] places single-token streaming deep in the memory-bound region of the roofline (@fig-patterson-roofline) [@williams2009roofline]. On the mobile manipulator's application processor it caps the intent model's fresh-evaluation rate, before any vision or decoding work, far below the rate of a joint controller that asks for a new command every millisecond (\ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking}). A model renewed that slowly can say where the arm should go, but it cannot close the loop on moving mass, so it proposes waypoints and a faster loop below it tracks them.

[The embodied batch size 1 constraint]{.heading-3-inline}
Cloud inference servers escape the memory wall by aggregating requests across hundreds of concurrent users into large batches ($B = 64\text{--}256$), multiplying arithmetic intensity by computing matrix-matrix products ($\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}$) rather than matrix-vector products. An embodied robot cannot use this luxury. It operates under the **embodied batch size 1 constraint**: the agent commands exactly one physical plant in real time. Batching across time introduces unrecoverable latency ($\Delta t = B \times t_{\text{sample}}$) that starves motor drives, while batching across requests is physically impossible on a single robot. Consequently, embodied deliberation is trapped at $B = 1$, making off-chip memory traffic the non-negotiable ceiling on inference cadence.

[^fn-hw-dram-bandwidth]: **Autoregressive DRAM Bandwidth Saturation**\index{GPU!memory bandwidth wall}: Sequential action tokens can trigger repeated full-model weight traffic when weights are nonresident and the decoder revisits the backbone; cache behavior and hardware determine the actual bandwidth ceiling. Action chunking is one way to reduce the number of full policy evaluations per unit of physical time.

This continuous data movement also carries an energy penalty. Fetching weights from off-chip DRAM consumes orders of magnitude more energy than the arithmetic computation itself ($\approx 10\text{--}20\,\text{pJ/bit}$ for LPDDR5 DRAM access versus $< 0.1\,\text{pJ/FLOP}$ for on-chip FP16 multiply-accumulate). That continuous memory traffic drains battery reserves, and the heat it leaves in the chassis raises the local ambient temperature of the joint actuators, shrinking the thermal winding margins codified in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.

::: {#fig-patterson-roofline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an example edge accelerator. Single-token weight streaming can be memory-bound; reuse across a chunk may increase work per byte. A separate real-time loop executes accepted waypoints between fresh model updates." fig-alt="Illustrative roofline diagram plotting arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput, with example points for token decoding and action chunking."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EMBODIED ROOFLINE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-patterson-roofline
# │ Goal:    show that embodied inference sits far inside the memory-bound regime
# │ Show:    arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an edge part
# │ How:     roof from the registry node; each workload amortizes the single-token
# │          sweep over the chapter's own chunk horizon H and denoising depth K
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim import Embodied

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
node = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet; the mobile manipulator's application processor
I_TOKEN = 1.0  # category: illustrative; FLOP/byte for a single-token weight sweep
H_CHUNK = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen; the machine's action-chunk horizon
K_DENOISE = 10  # category: illustrative; denoising steps per chunk for the diffusion policy

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
peak = node.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw = node.memory.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
ridge = peak / (bw / 1000)  # FLOP/byte
attainable = lambda ai: min(bw * ai / 1000, peak)

points = [
    ("Autoregressive VLA\n(single token)", I_TOKEN),
    (f"Action chunking\n(H = {H_CHUNK})", H_CHUNK * I_TOKEN),
    (f"Diffusion policy\n(H = {H_CHUNK}, K = {K_DENOISE})", H_CHUNK * K_DENOISE * I_TOKEN),
]

# ┌── 3. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = viz.plot_roofline(node)
COLORS = viz.COLORS
ax.set_ylim(peak * 0.0004, peak * 2)  # keep the single-token point on scale
for idx, (label, ai) in enumerate(points):
    y = attainable(ai)
    ax.plot(ai, y, "o", ms=8, color=COLORS["VioletLine"], zorder=11)
    # the lowest point has no room beneath the roof, so its label goes above
    if idx == 0:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 0.40, y * 4.0), "right", "bottom"
    else:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 2.4, y * 0.30), "left", "top"
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(ai, y),
        xytext=pos,
        fontsize=8,
        color=COLORS["VioletLine"],
        ha=ha,
        va=va,
        zorder=11,
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["VioletLine"], lw=0.9),
    )

# the reuse a workload would need before it left the memory-bound regime
ax.annotate(
    f"reuse must reach {ridge:.0f} FLOP/byte\nbefore compute binds",
    xy=(ridge, peak * 0.006),
    xytext=(ridge * 0.30, peak * 0.0012),
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    ha="right",
    zorder=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9),
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The roofline model in @fig-patterson-roofline formalizes the hardware boundary governing embodied inference by plotting attainable computational throughput against **arithmetic intensity** ($I$), defined as:
$$I = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes transferred from off-chip memory}}$$
For single-token autoregressive decoding, generating each subsequent action token requires evaluating a matrix-vector product $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$ across all model weights with batch size 1. In 16-bit floating-point precision (FP16, 2 bytes per parameter), each weight participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), yielding an arithmetic intensity of:
$$I_{\text{token}} = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
On the mobile manipulator's application processor (`node = RM.brain_soc`, an edge SoC with $\Pi_{\text{peak}} = 275\,\text{TFLOPs/s}$ FP16 compute and $\beta_{\text{mem}} = 204\,\text{GB/s}$ memory bandwidth), the hardware ridge point occurs at:
$$I_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{\Pi_{\text{peak}}}{\beta_{\text{mem}}} = \frac{275 \times 10^{12}\,\text{FLOPs/s}}{204 \times 10^9\,\text{Bytes/s}} \approx 1348\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
Because single-token autoregressive decoding operates at $I_{\text{token}} = 1.0 \ll I_{\text{ridge}}$, it sits trapped deep in the memory-bound regime, throttled to $\beta_{\text{mem}} \cdot I_{\text{token}} \approx 0.204\,\text{TFLOPs/s}$—less than 0.1 percent of the silicon's arithmetic peak. For the physical robot, the consequences of this arithmetic starvation are severe: generating a single 7-DoF action from a 7-billion parameter model via sequential token generation requires streaming the full weight footprint seven times, requiring nearly $500\,\text{ms}$ per composite command. Attempting to evaluate this autoregressive loop directly inside the control path starves the motor drives, turning continuous trajectory tracking into jerky, stuttering limit cycles that cannot stabilize moving masses or track dynamic objects.

Action chunking and trajectory diffusion overcome this bottleneck by amortizing weight transfers across multi-step outputs:

* **Action Chunking ($H = 16$):** Predicting a chunk of $H=16$ future waypoints in a single forward pass reuses model parameters across 16 outputs, increasing arithmetic intensity sixteenfold to $I \approx 16\,\text{FLOP/byte}$ and lifting attainable throughput to $3.26\,\text{TFLOPs/s}$ (1.2 percent of peak). Crucially, action chunking amortizes the massive 7B-parameter weight streaming bandwidth ($700\text{ GB/s} \to 44\text{ GB/s}$) over physical wall-clock time.
* **Diffusion Policy ($H = 16, K = 10$):** Running $K = 10$ iterative refinement steps exclusively over the compact action head (typically 50M parameters, rather than the 7B backbone) yields high temporal precision without re-streaming the massive visual foundation model backbone on every denoising tick. While this is a $160\times$ throughput leap over single-token decoding, the workload remains memory-bound on this flagship SoC because $I < I_{\text{ridge}}$. By contrast, on an entry-level edge processor ($\Pi_{\text{peak}} = 32\,\text{TFLOPs/s}, \beta_{\text{mem}} = 100\,\text{GB/s} \implies I_{\text{ridge}} = 320\,\text{FLOP/byte}$), that same $I = 160\,\text{FLOP/byte}$ reaches $16\,\text{TFLOPs/s}$, claiming fully 50 percent of the compute ceiling.

### Action chunking {#sec-brain-action-chunking}

Classical digital control loops evaluate sensors and compute scalar feedback corrections synchronously at high rates ($100\text{--}1000\,\text{Hz}$). In physical AI architectures driven by multi-billion-parameter neural networks, however, single-step closed-loop evaluation at millisecond cadences is physically infeasible due to the memory wall and compute latency. If a neural policy requiring $100\,\text{ms}$ of inference time were evaluated strictly for single-step commands, the physical plant would spend $99\,\text{ms}$ out of every $100\,\text{ms}$ interval unguided, leading to discrete limit cycles and instability. Instead, physical AI decouples deliberation from tracking by predicting continuous trajectory segments.

[Supply rate vs. closed-loop reaction latency]{.heading-3-inline}
To supply dense waypoints despite slow full-model inference, modern physical AI policies employ **action chunking**\index{Action chunking!temporal trajectory} (\ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Each chunk then crosses the proposal boundary as one packet, the chunk payload of @sec-nervous-cadences. However, systems engineers must never confuse **setpoint supply cadence** with **closed-loop reaction bandwidth**:

* *Setpoint supply cadence* ($f_{\text{supply}} = 1/\Delta t_{\text{step}} = 50\,\text{Hz}$): The rate at which the trajectory queue delivers discrete waypoints to the joint servo loop.
* *Policy replanning rate* ($f_{\text{replan}} = 20\,\text{Hz}$, period $T_{\text{replan}} = 50\,\text{ms}$): The cadence at which the neural backbone evaluates new sensory frames.
* *Closed-loop reaction latency* ($T_{\text{reaction}} = T_{\text{replan}} + t_{\text{infer}} = 50\,\text{ms} + 40\,\text{ms} = 90\,\text{ms}$): The true physical delay before an unmodeled external disturbance or obstacle perceived by the camera can alter the proposed path.

Action chunking solves actuator starvation (supply rate), not feedback latency. If an unexpected obstacle appears immediately after camera exposure, the robot continues executing the open-loop chunk for up to $90\,\text{ms}$ before a revised proposal arrives. Disturbance rejection and obstacle compliance cannot rely on chunk policies; they must be guaranteed by the 1 kHz real-time Nervous System.

A chunking policy (such as Action Chunking with Transformers [ACT], Diffusion Policy, or Flow Matching) generates its whole chunk of $H$ setpoints in one backbone pass followed, for an iterative decoder, by $K = 10\text{--}16$ refinement steps.

To understand why physical AI systems rely on trajectory diffusion rather than standard regression, consider the problem of multimodality in human demonstration data. Standard behavioral cloning trains a deterministic network using mean squared error (MSE) loss: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \|\pi(\mathbf{o}) - \mathbf{a}\|^2$. This objective implicitly assumes a unimodal Gaussian conditional distribution. In real-world manipulation, however, demonstrations are inherently multimodal: faced with an obstacle, a human demonstrator may navigate either to the left or to the right with equal probability. Under MSE loss, minimizing error across both modes forces the network to predict the conditional expectation—the arithmetic mean of the two trajectories—directing the robot straight into the obstacle.

Diffusion policies resolve mode averaging by representing actions as a continuous multi-step trajectory tensor $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a}$, where $H$ is the trajectory horizon and $d_a$ is the action dimension (such as 6-DoF end-effector delta poses and gripper states). Training optimizes the score-matching loss over demonstration trajectories:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{diffusion}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{k, \mathbf{A}^{(0)}, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[ \left\| \boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\left(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_k}\mathbf{A}^{(0)} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \, k, \, \mathbf{o}\right) \right\|^2 \right]$$
where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$ and $\mathbf{o} = \mathbf{h}_{\text{context}}$ is the visual-semantic conditioning vector computed from the VLA backbone. By Tweedie's formula, the noise-prediction head directly estimates the score of the perturbed trajectory distribution:
$$\nabla_{\mathbf{A}^{(k)}} \log p_k\left(\mathbf{A}^{(k)} \mid \mathbf{o}\right) = -\frac{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\left(\mathbf{A}^{(k)}, k, \mathbf{o}\right)}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}}$$
Denoising begins by sampling pure Gaussian noise $\mathbf{A}^{(K)} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. Over $K = 10\text{--}16$ discrete refinement iterations, the learned noise-prediction head $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{A}^{(k)}, k, \mathbf{o})$ iteratively strips noise from the trajectory tensor.[^fn-math-diffusion-denoising] This transforms unconstrained Gaussian noise into a smooth, kinematically consistent trajectory chunk $\mathbf{A}^{(0)} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}]$, faithfully capturing complex multimodal behaviors without mode collapse.

Crucially from an ML systems perspective, the $K$ iterative refinement steps run **exclusively on the compact action head** (typically a $\sim 50\text{M}$-parameter temporal 1D-U-Net or lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) or transformer decoder), **never on the 7-billion-parameter foundation model backbone**. The 7B vision-language backbone executes only once per replanning cycle to extract $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}}$, streaming its multi-gigabyte weight footprint across off-chip DRAM once every $50\text{--}200\,\text{ms}$.

Because the 50M action head occupies under $100\,\text{MB}$ in FP16 (or $\approx 25\,\text{MB}$ in INT4), its parameters and intermediate activation tensors fit comfortably within on-chip SRAM or system-level cache (SLC). The $K$ refinement passes proceed at high computational efficiency ($> 1\text{--}2\,\text{TB/s}$ SRAM bandwidth) without repeatedly saturating the off-chip DRAM bus. Furthermore, executing $K = 10\text{--}16$ iterative steps in standard eager-mode frameworks would dispatch hundreds of small layer kernels, incurring catastrophic **kernel launch overhead** ($\approx 5\text{--}15\,\mu\text{s}$ CPU-to-GPU launch latency per kernel) that serializes execution on host dispatch queues. Embodied runtimes eliminate this CPU overhead via **CUDA Graph capture** or compiled execution graphs (such as TensorRT engines or TorchDynamo ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation), executing the entire iterative denoising loop as a single hardware-scheduled task on device in $5\text{--}15\,\text{ms}$.

[^fn-math-diffusion-denoising]: **Diffusion policy reverse step algebra**: In score-based DDPM sampling, each reverse denoising step evaluates $\mathbf{A}^{(k-1)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_k}} \left( \mathbf{A}^{(k)} - \frac{1 - \alpha_k}{\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_k}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta \right) + \sigma_k \mathbf{z}$, where $\alpha_k$ and $\bar{\alpha}_k$ track the noise schedule and $\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$. Setting $\sigma_k = 0$ yields deterministic DDIM trajectories. Full mathematical derivations and schedule parameters are provided in @sec-training-decoder-costs and @sec-appendix-ml-diffusion.

[Flow matching vs. diffusion denoising]{.heading-3-inline}
While diffusion policies require $K = 10\text{--}16$ curved steps along score-based trajectories, modern flow-matching foundation models (such as Physical Intelligence $\pi_0$ [@black2024pi0] and NVIDIA Project GR00T) straighten probability paths into continuous vector fields using optimal transport and rectified flows. By integrating straight probability trajectories, flow matching can generate high-fidelity trajectory chunks in only $1\text{--}4$ Euler steps. Reducing action head evaluations from 16 steps to 2 steps slashes decode latency from $25\,\text{ms}$ to $3\,\text{ms}$, allowing multi-billion parameter foundation models to achieve $50\text{--}100\,\text{Hz}$ proposal rates.

::: {#dfn-brain-action-chunking .callout-definition title="Temporal action chunking"}

***Temporal action chunking***\index{Temporal action chunking!definition}\index{Action chunking!definition} is the policy formulation that predicts an entire horizon of $H$ future continuous actions $\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}]$ in a single neural evaluation or diffusion rollout, amortizing parameter memory transfers across extended physical execution windows.

1.  **Significance**: On a bandwidth-limited device, repeating a full model evaluation for every action can be too slow for millisecond control. Temporal action chunking can reuse a backbone evaluation across multiple waypoints; it does not make fresh observations or policy decisions arrive at the waypoint rate. A downstream controller tracks the accepted trajectory between model updates.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike single-step Markovian policies $\mathbf{a}_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \mathbf{o}_t)$ that re-evaluate the full neural network at every control step, action chunking deliberately generates multi-step feedforward trajectories, utilizing receding-horizon execution and blending across overlapping chunks to reconcile slow neural deliberation with fast closed-loop control.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Executing action chunks open-loop without continuous temporal smoothing or runtime safety filtering. Without smooth blending across overlapping chunk boundaries, switching between independently generated horizons injects acceleration jumps and torque shocks that excite mechanical gearbox resonances.

:::
For example, when a canonical bimanual manipulator threads a flexible USB cable (@fig-aloha-manipulator), it executes a 32-step action chunk, a longer chunk than the mobile manipulator uses. The policy emits coordinated 14-DoF joint setpoints that smoothly align both grippers, flex the cable, and insert the connector without pausing between individual control cycles.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sequence strip illustrating overlapping action chunk horizons of 32 steps with 12-step replanning and temporal ensembling."}

*Overlapping action chunks blend predictions across receding temporal execution windows.*
:::

However, action chunking introduces the problem of **chunk seam continuity**. Because each action chunk is generated independently from rolling sensory observations, the tail of chunk $k$ and the head of chunk $k+1$ may exhibit slight positional and velocity discrepancies. If a controller concatenated these chunks directly, the resulting step-discontinuities in acceleration would inject large jerk ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) into the physical linkages, inducing mechanical shock, acoustic vibration, cycloidal pin wear, and motor overcurrent faults.

To reduce discontinuities between overlapping chunks, systems can implement **temporal ensembling**\index{Temporal ensembling!trajectory smoothing}, blending overlapping trajectory predictions via exponentially weighted averaging:

$$\mathbf{a}_t = \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H-1)} w_i \, \mathbf{a}_{t \mid t-i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{\min(t, H-1)} w_i}, \quad w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)$$

where $\mathbf{a}_{t \mid t-i}$ represents the action predicted for time step $t$ by the action chunk initiated at time $t-i$, and $m > 0$ is a tunable temporal discount factor. The permission path interpolates the blended waypoints below the proposal boundary (@sec-nervous-cadences).

::: {.callout-perspective title="The temporal ensembling jerk trap"}
Exponentially weighted temporal ensembling guarantees positional ($C^0$) continuity by construction, but does not enforce continuity in velocity ($\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, $C^1$) or acceleration ($\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$, $C^2$). When successive action chunks disagree in trajectory slope due to sensor noise or latent representation drift, ensembling creates an instantaneous corner in the reference trajectory. In high-gain joint PD tracking ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{K}_p \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{K}_d \dot{\mathbf{e}}$), a step change in commanded velocity produces an impulsive torque spike that excites drive resonances and can trigger inverter overcurrent faults. For example, in a $1000\,\text{Hz}$ joint servo loop ($\Delta t = 1\,\text{ms}$) with derivative gain $\mathbf{K}_d = 40\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$, an instantaneous velocity discontinuity of just $\Delta \dot{q} = 0.5\,\text{rad/s}$ between successive chunks commands an impulsive torque step of $\Delta \tau \approx \mathbf{K}_d \Delta \dot{q} / \Delta t \approx 20\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ within a single servo cycle. Such sudden torque transients excite mechanical gearbox harmonics, accelerate cycloidal pin fatigue, and can trip inverter overcurrent protection. Downstream controllers must pass blended setpoints through an online continuous interpolator (such as a quintic Hermite spline or second-order low-pass filter) to enforce $C^2$ continuity before setpoints cross the causal boundary.
:::

This operational tension between neural deliberation capacity and physical control latency defines the central scaling frontier of modern robotic brains (@fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline). To understand this frontier, consider the fundamental distinction between two architectural paradigms:

* **Vision-Language Models (VLMs):** Multimodal foundation models (such as GPT-4V, PaLM-E, and Gemini) ingest camera frames and text prompts to output discrete linguistic tokens ($y \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{text}}$). While VLMs excel at open-world semantic scene understanding, object categorization, and task decomposition, their representations live in abstract linguistic space without spatial coordinates, joint torque limits, or physical time awareness.
* **Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs):** Physical AI policies (such as RT-1, RT-2, OpenVLA, and $\pi_0$) extend multimodal transformers directly into the physical world. Rather than producing descriptive text, a VLA grounds visual observations and natural language instructions into physical robotic actions ($\mathbf{a}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_a}$)—such as 6-DoF end-effector delta poses, gripper open/close triggers, or continuous joint setpoints.

Between 2020 and 2023, pioneering vision-language-action (VLA)\index{Vision-language-action model} models such as RT-1 [@brohan2023rt1], RT-2 [@brohan2023rt2], and OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla] tokenized continuous actions into discrete bins (typically 256 uniform bins per dimension), predicting one action step per autoregressive forward pass. However, because each forward pass requires streaming every model parameter from DRAM across the silicon memory bus, policy update rates collapsed as model capacity scaled ($f_{\text{action}} \propto 1 / M_{\text{weights}}$)—trapping multi-billion-parameter models behind an insurmountable "deliberation wall" ($1\text{--}3\,\text{Hz}$) that fell far below the $50\,\text{Hz}$ closed-loop threshold required for dynamic contact and reactive manipulation.

Action chunking fundamentally decoupled deliberation from actuation frequency. Instead of streaming billions of parameters for every low-level setpoint, architectures such as ACT [@zhao2023learning], Diffusion Policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy], and modern flow-matching foundation models (e.g., Physical Intelligence $\pi_0$ [@black2024pi0] and NVIDIA Project GR00T) evaluate their large perceptual backbones periodically to generate entire multi-step action trajectories ($H = 16\text{--}64$). Compact, highly optimized generative action heads then denoise or integrate these trajectories at $50\text{--}100\,\text{Hz}$, shattering the autoregressive memory wall and reconciling multi-billion parameter semantic reasoning with millisecond closed-loop physical control.

::: {#fig-03-vla-scaling-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Embodied Brain Frontier**: Foundation policy parameter capacity ($M_{\\text{weights}}$, log scale, $20\\,\\text{M}$ to $100\\,\\text{B}$ parameters) vs. onboard closed-loop action frequency ($f_{\\text{action}}$, log scale, $0.5\\,\\text{Hz}$ to $200\\,\\text{Hz}$) across robotic policies (2020–2026). Single-token discrete autoregressive policies (RT-1, RT-2-PaLM-E, RT-2-PaLI-X, OpenVLA Base) hit an insurmountable memory wall ($f \\propto 1/M_{\\text{weights}}$) bounded by DRAM streaming bandwidth ($B_{\\text{mem}} / M_{\\text{weights}}$), stranding large models at $1\\text{--}3\\,\\text{Hz}$. Continuous action chunking (ACT, Diffusion Policy) and flow-matching dual-system architectures (Physical Intelligence $\\pi_0$, NVIDIA Project GR00T, 2026 dual-brain SoCs) shatter this bottleneck: decoupling multi-step chunk generation ($H = 16\\text{--}64$) from low-latency generative action heads enables multi-billion parameter foundation models to achieve $50\\text{--}100\\,\\text{Hz}$ real-time reactive control." fig-alt="Log-log plot comparing model parameter count from 15 million to 120 billion on the horizontal axis against onboard action frequency from 0.35 Hz to 210 Hz on the vertical axis. Highlights the steep performance drop of single-token autoregressive models along the deliberation wall vs. the high-frequency frontier of action chunking and flow matching architectures reaching 50 to 100 Hz."}
